title: Two months of left iliac fossa pain and bloody diarrhoea in a 25-year-old man
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 25-year-old accountant in general practice with 2 months of left iliac fossa pain, diarrhoea with blood and mucus, weight loss and tender lumps on his shins. The candidate then interprets his blood tests, stool tests and colonoscopy with biopsy report, recognises ulcerative colitis (proctosigmoiditis) that is not acute severe, plans first-line management with the gastroenterologist, and explains the complications and extraintestinal manifestations.
focus: Recognising and confirming inflammatory bowel disease in a young adult with chronic bloody diarrhoea, and distinguishing ulcerative colitis from Crohn's disease
stem: You are a general practitioner in a busy metropolitan practice. Andrew (Andy) Chase, a 25-year-old accountant, has come to see you with abdominal pain.
tasks: Take a focused history from Andy and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the results of Andy's blood tests and stool tests, and the report of the colonoscopy and biopsies done by the gastroenterologist. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Andrew (Andy) Chase, a 25-year-old accountant. You are friendly and relaxed on the surface but worried underneath, mostly because of your dad. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "Hey doc, I've just been having some tummy pain..."

The pain (give only when asked):

  • In the lower left side of your tummy. It doesn't go anywhere else.
  • Sharp and aching. About 6 out of 10.
  • Started about 2 months ago, came on gradually, and is there all the time. It is slowly getting worse. You have never had anything like it before.
  • Nothing makes it better or worse: not eating, not opening your bowels, not moving.
  • It is affecting your work: your boss has told you that you aren't performing like you usually do.

Bowels and other symptoms (give only when asked):

  • Diarrhoea for the same 2 months: loose stools about 4 or 5 times a day, sometimes once overnight, and you often have to rush to the toilet.
  • There is blood and mucus in the stool. If asked more: the blood is red and mixed through the stool. The stools are not greasy, pale or hard to flush.
  • "Bumps on my shins": a few sore, red lumps on both shins that came up about 3 weeks ago. You haven't knocked them.
  • You have lost about 5 kg in 2 months without trying (from 75 kg). You feel tired all the time.
  • No fevers or night sweats.
  • No red or sore eyes, no mouth ulcers, no joint pain or swelling.
  • No nausea, vomiting, constipation or bloating.
  • No dizziness, breathlessness or racing heart.

Possible causes (only if asked): no change to medicines or diet. No overseas or rural travel, no camping or tank water. Nobody around you is unwell. No antibiotics or anti-inflammatories (Nurofen) recently. No particular stress apart from work noticing you're off.

Past medical history: asthma as a child, none now. Vaccinations up to date.

Medications: none, including nothing over the counter. Allergies: none known.

Family history: your father died of bowel (colorectal) cancer at 65. Your mother has Hashimoto's (an underactive thyroid). Nobody in the family has inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's or colitis) or coeliac disease.

Social history:

  • Lives with your girlfriend in the inner west; she is very supportive.
  • Works full time as an accountant.
  • Drinks socially on weekends. Never smoked. No recreational drugs.
  • Balanced diet; you go to the gym 3 times a week.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you first thought it was "a bug", but it hasn't gone away. Since the blood started you have been worried it could be cancer like your dad's, although you haven't said this to anyone. You want to know what is going on and get it fixed so you can get back on top of work.

Question to raise once in Part 1 (when blood or your family history comes up): "Could this be cancer, like Dad had?" Accept an honest answer: it is less likely at your age, but it needs proper tests, including a look inside the bowel.

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: alert, comfortable at rest, slim. Not pale or jaundiced. Well hydrated. Weight 70 kg, height 178 cm.
  • Observations: HR 84 regular, BP 122/76, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C.
  • Hands: no clubbing, no palmar pallor.
  • Eyes: no redness, no conjunctival pallor, no jaundice.
  • Mouth: no ulcers.
  • Abdomen: not distended, no scars. Soft. Mild tenderness in the left iliac fossa, no guarding or rebound. No masses. Liver and spleen not palpable. Bowel sounds normal. Renal angles not tender.
  • Shins: four tender, raised, red-purple nodules 1 to 3 cm across over both anterior shins. No ulceration.
  • Joints: no swelling or tenderness of the hands, knees or ankles.
  • Perianal inspection and digital rectal examination (if offered, with consent and a chaperone): no skin tags, fissures, fistulae or abscess. Mildly tender rectum, no mass. Blood and mucus on the glove.
  • Heart and chest: normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and confirms Andy's identity.
Opens with an open question, uses plain language, acknowledges the effect on his work and his worry about his father, and summarises back to him.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: lower left abdomen, no radiation.
Character and severity: sharp and aching, 6/10, affecting his work.
Onset and course: gradual over 2 months, constant and worsening, never before; nothing makes it better or worse.

check.x: Characterises the bowel symptoms:

kids.x: Diarrhoea: frequency (4 to 5 a day), nocturnal stools and urgency.
Asks specifically about blood and mucus: red blood mixed through the stool, with mucus.
Asks whether the stools are greasy, pale or hard to flush (no).

check.x: Asks about systemic symptoms: weight loss (5 kg in 2 months), fatigue, fevers and night sweats.
Screens for extraintestinal features:

kids.x: Skin: the tender red lumps on both shins for 3 weeks.
Eyes: redness or pain (none).
Mouth ulcers (none).
Joint pain or swelling (none).

check.x: Screens the other gastrointestinal and anaemia symptoms: nausea, vomiting, bloating, constipation, dizziness, breathlessness or palpitations (none).
Asks about infective and other triggers: travel, sick contacts, change in diet or medicines, recent antibiotics or NSAIDs, and stressors (none).
Takes a family history: father died of colorectal cancer at 65, mother has Hashimoto's thyroiditis, and asks specifically about IBD and coeliac disease (none).
Takes the past history, medicines and allergies: childhood asthma, vaccinations up to date, no regular or over-the-counter medicines, no allergies.
Takes a social history: smoking (never), alcohol (social), drugs (none), full-time accountant, lives with a supportive girlfriend, diet and exercise.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations, including the fear of cancer like his father's, and answers it honestly (less likely at his age, but needs investigation including colonoscopy).
Examination
Asks for vital signs (HR, BP, temperature, RR, SpO2) and weight, and notes he is afebrile, not tachycardic and has lost about 5 kg.
Inspects generally and examines the hands, eyes, mouth and joints: pallor, clubbing, red eyes, mouth ulcers, joint swelling and hydration.
Examines the abdomen: inspection, palpation for tenderness, guarding and masses (soft, mild LIF tenderness, no mass), liver and spleen, percussion and bowel sounds.
Inspects the shins and describes tender, raised, red-purple nodules on both shins, consistent with erythema nodosum.
Offers a perianal inspection and digital rectal examination with consent and a chaperone (no tags, fissures or fistulae; blood and mucus on the glove, no mass).
Interpretation

Interprets the colonoscopy and biopsies as ulcerative colitis of the rectum and distal sigmoid (proctosigmoiditis): continuous inflammation starting at the anal verge, limited to the mucosa, with crypt architectural distortion showing chronic colitis.
Explains why this is not Crohn's disease: no skip lesions, a normal terminal ileum and proximal colon, mucosal rather than transmural inflammation, no granulomas, and no perianal disease.
check.d: Do not credit cobblestoning, linear ulcers or strictures as features of this report: they are Crohn's features and the report states they are absent.

check.x: Interprets the stool tests: no bacterial, parasitic (including Giardia) or C. difficile infection, so infective colitis is excluded; calprotectin 720 confirms active bowel inflammation.
Interprets the blood tests:

kids.x: Mild microcytic anaemia with low ferritin and transferrin saturation: iron deficiency from blood loss.
Raised CRP, ESR and platelets: active inflammation.
Negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA makes coeliac disease unlikely; normal LFTs (including ALP), albumin and TSH.

check.x: Assesses severity on today's findings: 4 to 5 bloody stools a day (fewer than 6), afebrile, HR 82 (under 90), Hb 124 (above 105) and ESR 28 (below 30), so this is not acute severe colitis (Truelove and Witts) and can be managed as an outpatient.
Gives the differentials with a feature for or against each:

kids.x: Infective colitis, including giardiasis: no travel or contacts, stool tests negative.
Coeliac disease: no bloating or greasy stools, serology negative, and it does not typically cause visible blood in the stool.
Colorectal cancer: father's history and weight loss, but young, and no mass or dysplasia at colonoscopy.
Irritable bowel syndrome: a diagnosis of exclusion; blood, weight loss, nocturnal stools and raised calprotectin rule it out.

check.x: Management
Explains the diagnosis in plain words: long-term inflammation of the lining of the lower bowel that flares and settles, not caused by anything he did, not catching, and controllable with treatment.
Liaises with the gastroenterologist for shared care and an agreed treatment plan.
Plans first-line rectal mesalazine as an enema or foam (which reaches the sigmoid) plus oral mesalazine, agreed with the gastroenterologist.
check.d: Credit rectal plus oral mesalazine without exact doses. Do not credit routine first-line oral steroids or antibiotics.

check.x: Plans review in 2 to 4 weeks, with the specialist adding a corticosteroid if there is no response, and explains that long-term maintenance mesalazine continues once in remission.

Treats the iron deficiency: IV iron (e.g. ferric carboxymaltose) is preferred because his colitis is active; oral iron (e.g. alternate-day dosing) is acceptable for mild anaemia if tolerated. Rechecks FBC and iron studies.

Plans drug safety and monitoring: baseline and periodic renal function on mesalazine, avoids NSAIDs (paracetamol for the shin pain), and reviews vaccinations in case immunosuppression is needed later.
Addresses his wellbeing: the impact on work (medical certificate if needed), support from Crohn's & Colitis Australia, and that the erythema nodosum usually settles as the colitis is controlled.
Answers his question about complications in the bowel:

kids.x: Acute severe colitis and toxic megacolon, which can lead to perforation.
Severe bleeding.
A higher risk of colorectal cancer over time, which is why he will need surveillance colonoscopy, with his father's history taken into account.

check.x: Names at least three extraintestinal manifestations from different systems: joints and bone (enteropathic arthritis, osteoporosis), eyes (episcleritis, anterior uveitis), skin (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum), liver (primary sclerosing cholangitis), and tells him to seek same-day review if any of these appear (red painful eye or blurred vision, jaundice, a skin ulcer, a hot swollen joint).
Safety netting

Tells him in plain words to go to the ED the same day (or call 000 if he collapses) for 6 or more bloody stools a day, fever, a racing heart, severe or worsening pain or a swollen tummy, dizziness or fainting, or being unable to keep fluids down.

Arranges follow-up: GP review in 2 to 4 weeks with repeat FBC, iron studies and renal function; the gastroenterology appointment; surveillance colonoscopy planned by the specialist; written information.

part2.lead: Andy comes back two weeks later. Today he reports 4 to 5 loose stools a day with blood, about once overnight. Observations today: temperature 36.8 °C, HR 82, BP 120/76, RR 14, SpO2 99%, weight 70 kg. Here are the blood and stool results from the tests you arranged at his first visit, and the report of the colonoscopy and biopsies the gastroenterologist did last week.
part2.patient:
When the candidate explains the diagnosis or the plan, ask once each:

  • "So is this what Dad had? Am I going to get cancer?"
  • "Will I have to be on treatment forever?"

You are relieved that it is not cancer and that there is a treatment plan. If the candidate uses jargon such as "5-ASA" or "extraintestinal" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.result: Collected at the first visit, before any treatment. Andy was eating a normal diet containing gluten.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 124 with MCV 78 and MCH 25: mild microcytic anaemia. Ferritin 18, iron 7 and transferrin saturation 10% are low: iron deficiency. Platelets 468, CRP 24 and ESR 28 are raised. UEC, LFTs (including ALP and GGT) and albumin are normal. tTG-IgA is negative with a normal total IgA, so the negative result is valid. TSH is normal.
  • For Andy: iron deficiency from chronic blood loss in the stool, with a systemic inflammatory response (thrombocytosis reflects active inflammation and iron deficiency). Coeliac disease is unlikely, and thyroid disease (mother's Hashimoto's) does not explain his fatigue or weight loss. Normal ALP and GGT give no evidence of primary sclerosing cholangitis. Hb above 105 and ESR below 30 are not acute severe criteria.
  • What it changes: iron replacement with a recheck; baseline renal function before mesalazine.

labs.title: Full blood count and inflammatory markers

handover.label: Stool tests
handover.result: Single stool sample collected at the first visit, before any treatment. Lab comment: no enteric pathogens detected.
handover.model:
• Read: multiplex PCR and culture are negative for Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli. C. difficile toxin gene not detected. Giardia, Cryptosporidium and Entamoeba histolytica not detected, and no ova, cysts or parasites seen. Faecal calprotectin 720 µg/g, well above 50.
  • For Andy: infective colitis, including giardiasis and C. difficile, is excluded, which fits his lack of travel, contacts and antibiotics and a 2-month course. The high calprotectin confirms neutrophil-driven inflammation of the bowel wall, which separates organic disease from IBS but does not distinguish UC from Crohn's.
  • What it changes: infection must be excluded before treating colitis, especially before steroids. Calprotectin becomes a baseline for monitoring his response.

handover.label: Colonoscopy and biopsy report
handover.result:
Examination: colonoscopy to the terminal ileum with biopsies, under sedation. Bowel preparation good.

Clinical details: 25-year-old man. 2 months of left iliac fossa pain and diarrhoea with blood and mucus, 5 kg weight loss, tender nodules on both shins. Father had colorectal cancer at 65. Stool pathogens negative; faecal calprotectin 720 µg/g.

Macroscopic findings:

  • Perianal region and rectal examination: no skin tags, fissures or fistulae.
  • Rectum and distal sigmoid colon (anal verge to 25 cm, across the rectosigmoid junction): continuous, circumferential mucosal erythema and granularity with loss of the vascular pattern, contact bleeding and superficial ulceration. No deep, linear or aphthous ulcers, no cobblestoning, no strictures. Sharp transition to normal mucosa at 25 cm.
  • Proximal sigmoid, descending, transverse and ascending colon and caecum: normal mucosa. No skip lesions.
  • Terminal ileum: intubated; normal.
  • No mass lesions.

Histology:

  • Rectum and sigmoid (10 cm and 20 cm): crypt architectural distortion with crypt atrophy, irregular crypt spacing and crypt shortening. Active inflammation limited to the mucosa. No granulomas. No dysplasia.
  • Descending, transverse and ascending colon, terminal ileum (step biopsies): normal mucosa.

Conclusion: continuous chronic active colitis from the anal verge to 25 cm, limited to the mucosa, with chronic architectural changes. Proximal colon and terminal ileum normal. No granulomas or dysplasia. For clinicopathological correlation.
handover.model:
• Read: inflammation starts at the anal verge and is continuous and circumferential to 25 cm, with an abrupt margin and normal colon and terminal ileum beyond. Biopsies show crypt distortion, atrophy, irregular spacing and shortening (chronicity, not an acute infection) with inflammation confined to the mucosa. No granulomas, skip lesions, deep or linear ulcers, cobblestoning, strictures or perianal disease. No dysplasia.
  • For Andy: ulcerative colitis limited to the rectum and sigmoid (proctosigmoiditis, left-sided in the Montreal classification). Every feature argues against Crohn's disease. Erythema nodosum is an extraintestinal manifestation.
  • What it changes: distal disease suits rectal mesalazine as an enema or foam (a suppository only reaches the rectum) combined with oral mesalazine. Extent sets his future cancer surveillance.

ask: You are now calling the gastroenterology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Andy Chase, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Andy now, here in general practice.
Andy asks what complications this condition can cause, in the bowel and elsewhere in the body. Please answer him, then tell me when he should go to the emergency department.
expect:
• Identify: self, GP; Andy Chase, 25.
  • Situation: colonoscopy and biopsies confirm distal colitis; requesting a shared treatment plan.
  • Background: 2 months of LIF pain, 4 to 5 bloody mucousy stools a day, 5 kg weight loss, fatigue, erythema nodosum. Father had colorectal cancer at 65; mother has Hashimoto's. Non-smoker, no medicines.
  • Assessment: continuous mucosal colitis from the rectum to 25 cm with crypt distortion, no granulomas or dysplasia: UC proctosigmoiditis. Stool pathogens and C. difficile negative; calprotectin 720. Hb 124 with iron deficiency; CRP 24, ESR 28, platelets 468. Coeliac serology, LFTs and TSH normal. Today 4 to 5 bloody stools a day, afebrile, HR 82: not acute severe.
  • Recommendation: agree to start rectal plus oral mesalazine and iron; early clinic review.

Most likely: ulcerative colitis, proctosigmoiditis. 2 months of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea, LIF pain, weight loss, fatigue and erythema nodosum at a typical age, a family history of autoimmune disease, and continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum with crypt distortion.

  • Crohn's colitis: against: continuous rather than skip lesions, normal terminal ileum, mucosal only, no granulomas, no perianal disease.
  • Infective colitis or giardiasis: against: no travel or contacts, 2-month course, stool tests negative.
  • Coeliac disease: against: no bloating or greasy stools, bloody stools, tTG-IgA negative with normal IgA.
  • Colorectal cancer: for: father's history, weight loss, bleeding. Against: age 25, no mass or dysplasia.
  • IBS: against: a diagnosis of exclusion; blood, weight loss and calprotectin rule it out.

1. Explain in plain words: lifelong inflammation of the bowel lining that flares and settles; not his fault, not infectious, treatable.
  2. Severity: not acute severe (today 4 to 5 stools a day, afebrile, HR 82, Hb above 105, ESR below 30), so outpatient care.
  3. Shared care with the gastroenterologist.
  4. First line: rectal mesalazine enema or foam at night plus oral mesalazine; the combination is more effective. Review in 2 to 4 weeks; if no response, the specialist adds a corticosteroid. Long-term maintenance mesalazine once in remission.
  5. Iron: IV iron preferred while the colitis is active (oral acceptable if mild and tolerated); recheck FBC and iron studies.
  6. Safety: baseline and periodic renal function on mesalazine; avoid NSAIDs; review vaccinations.
  7. Support: medical certificate if needed, Crohn's & Colitis Australia.
  8. Follow-up: GP review in 2 to 4 weeks with FBC, iron studies and UEC; gastroenterology review; surveillance colonoscopy set by the specialist; written information.

Bowel complications: acute severe colitis and toxic megacolon with risk of perforation; severe bleeding; higher colorectal cancer risk over time (more with extensive or long-standing disease or PSC), so surveillance colonoscopy.

Elsewhere (at least 3): joints (arthritis, osteoporosis especially with steroids), eyes (episcleritis, anterior uveitis), skin (erythema nodosum, as he has; pyoderma gangrenosum), liver (PSC, with a risk of cholangiocarcinoma). Seek same-day review if any appear: red painful eye or blurred vision, jaundice, a skin ulcer, a hot swollen joint.

Go to ED the same day, or call 000 if he collapses: 6 or more bloody stools a day, fever, racing heart, severe pain or a swollen tummy, dizziness, not keeping fluids down.

ddx.for: Two months of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with LIF pain, weight loss, fatigue and erythema nodosum, and continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 25 cm with crypt distortion.
Young adult with weight loss, erythema nodosum and raised inflammatory markers.
ddx.against: Continuous inflammation from the rectum, normal terminal ileum, inflammation confined to the mucosa, no granulomas and no perianal disease.

ddx.for: Diarrhoea with blood and mucus and LIF pain.
ddx.against: No travel, sick contacts or antibiotics, a 2-month course, and negative stool PCR, culture, C. difficile and parasite tests.

ddx.for: Diarrhoea, weight loss and fatigue, with a mother who has autoimmune thyroid disease.
ddx.against: Blood in the stool, no bloating or greasy stools, and a negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA.

ddx.for: Rectal bleeding, 5 kg weight loss and iron deficiency, with a father who died of colorectal cancer at 65.
ddx.against: Age 25, and colonoscopy found no mass, with no dysplasia on biopsy.

ddx.for: Young man with abdominal pain and diarrhoea and work pressure.
ddx.against: Blood in the stool, nocturnal stools, weight loss, anaemia and a calprotectin of 720 exclude a functional diagnosis.

guide:
In Part 1, Andy gives the history only when asked, and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The shin lumps are mentioned only if the candidate asks about skin, rashes or lumps, or examines the legs. If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the results will be given in Part 2. Andy raises his cancer question once.

In Part 2, hand over all three results together, then ask the four questions in order. Andy asks his two questions when the candidate explains the plan. The source case has two examiner questions (complications, and extraintestinal manifestations); both are covered by question 4. Accept any reasonable equivalent wording for the extent of disease ("proctosigmoiditis", "distal" or "left-sided" UC). Do not credit cobblestoning, linear ulcers or strictures as features of this report.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain and stools, asks directly about blood and mucus, weight loss and nocturnal symptoms, screens the extraintestinal features and finds the shin lumps, takes the family history of colorectal cancer and autoimmune disease, and asks about travel, contacts and medicines. They take vital signs and weight, examine the abdomen and shins, and offer a chaperoned rectal examination. In Part 2 they read the colonoscopy as continuous mucosal colitis from the rectum, which is ulcerative colitis, and explain why it is not Crohn's. They note that infection has been excluded, recognise iron deficiency and active inflammation, and use objective criteria to show this is not acute severe colitis. They start rectal plus oral mesalazine with the gastroenterologist and name the complications and extraintestinal manifestations clearly.

A borderline candidate takes a pain history without asking about blood or weight loss, misses the erythema nodosum, does not offer a rectal examination, calls the report "colitis" without naming UC or explaining why it is not Crohn's, forgets that infection must be excluded, starts oral steroids or antibiotics first line, or gives vague safety netting.
explain:
Diagnosis: ulcerative colitis, proctosigmoiditis

Andy has 2 months of left iliac fossa pain with bloody, mucousy diarrhoea, urgency, nocturnal stools, 5 kg weight loss and fatigue, plus erythema nodosum. This is chronic inflammatory diarrhoea, and in a 25-year-old the leading cause is inflammatory bowel disease. His mother's autoimmune thyroid disease fits a family tendency to autoimmunity, and UC is more common in people who have never smoked. Colonoscopy shows continuous inflammation from the anal verge to 25 cm, limited to the mucosa, with crypt distortion, atrophy, irregular spacing and shortening (signs of chronicity) and a normal proximal colon and terminal ileum. This is ulcerative colitis of the rectum and sigmoid (proctosigmoiditis), within the left-sided (E2) group of the Montreal classification.

Crohn's disease versus ulcerative colitis

FeatureCrohn's diseaseUlcerative colitis
SymptomsMore pain (often right iliac fossa), weight loss, B12 deficiencyMore bloody, mucousy diarrhoea, urgency; left iliac fossa
DistributionAnywhere from mouth to anus; skip lesions; terminal ileumContinuous from the rectum, extending proximally
DepthTransmural: fistulae, strictures, abscessesMucosal only
EndoscopyAphthous and linear ulcers, cobblestoning, stricturesErythema, granularity, loss of vascular pattern, superficial ulcers, pseudopolyps
HistologyGranulomasCrypt distortion and crypt abscesses, no granulomas
Perianal diseaseCommonUncommon
ComplicationsFistulae, strictures, perianal abscessToxic megacolon; higher colorectal cancer risk; pyoderma gangrenosum and PSC more strongly associated

Pseudopolyps are islands of regenerating mucosa left after ulceration; they are not neoplastic.

Differentials

  • Infective colitis (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, STEC, C. difficile, Giardia, amoebiasis) must be excluded with stool testing before UC is diagnosed or treated, and again at each flare. Andy had no travel or contacts and his tests were negative.
  • Coeliac disease would more often give bloating, greasy stools and iron deficiency without rectal bleeding; serology is valid only on a gluten-containing diet and with a normal total IgA.
  • Colorectal cancer is uncommon at 25, but rectal bleeding, weight loss and iron deficiency with a first-degree relative affected need colonoscopy.
  • IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion: blood, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia and a raised calprotectin are red flags against it.

Investigations

FBC, UEC, LFTs, CRP and ESR, iron studies and coeliac serology; stool microscopy, culture or PCR with C. difficile testing and ova, cysts and parasites; faecal calprotectin; then colonoscopy with biopsies, which makes the diagnosis and sets the extent. Andy's iron deficiency anaemia reflects blood loss; thrombocytosis, CRP and ESR reflect inflammation; normal ALP and GGT give no sign of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

Severity

Acute severe UC (Truelove and Witts) is 6 or more bloody stools a day plus at least one sign of systemic toxicity: temperature above 37.8 °C, HR above 90, Hb below 105 g/L or ESR above 30. It needs hospital admission, IV corticosteroids, VTE prophylaxis and early gastroenterology and colorectal surgical input. Andy meets none of the systemic criteria and has 4 to 5 stools a day, so his disease is mild to moderate and managed as an outpatient.

Management (eTG Ulcerative colitis)

  • Induction for mild to moderate distal UC: aminosalicylates (5-ASA). Rectal mesalazine reaches the inflamed segment directly: suppositories treat the rectum, while enemas or foam reach the sigmoid and descending colon. Combined rectal and oral mesalazine is more effective than either alone.
  • If there is no response within a few weeks, the specialist adds a corticosteroid (rectal or oral), then considers immunomodulators or advanced therapies for steroid-dependent or refractory disease. Before immunosuppression, check vaccinations and screen for hepatitis B, TB and other infections.
  • Maintenance: continue mesalazine long term once in remission; it reduces flares and probably the colorectal cancer risk.
  • Monitoring: mesalazine can rarely cause interstitial nephritis, so check renal function at baseline and periodically.
  • Supportive: treat iron deficiency (IV iron preferred in active disease), avoid NSAIDs (they can trigger flares), consider bone health if steroids are used, and offer psychosocial support (Crohn's & Colitis Australia). Erythema nodosum usually parallels bowel activity and settles as the colitis is controlled.

Complications

  • Intestinal: acute severe colitis, toxic megacolon and perforation; haemorrhage; colorectal cancer (risk rises with duration, extent, severity of inflammation, PSC and a family history of colorectal cancer); PSC-related cholangiocarcinoma.
  • Extraintestinal: musculoskeletal (enteropathic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, osteoporosis, clubbing); eyes (episcleritis, anterior uveitis); skin (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum); hepatobiliary (primary sclerosing cholangitis); also VTE risk during flares.

Safety netting and follow-up

Andy should go to the ED the same day for signs of a severe flare (6 or more bloody stools a day, fever, racing heart, severe pain or a swollen tummy, dizziness, or not keeping fluids down) and seek same-day review for a red painful eye, jaundice, a skin ulcer or a hot swollen joint. GP review in 2 to 4 weeks rechecks his blood count, iron and renal function. The gastroenterologist plans surveillance colonoscopy, which in colitis beyond the rectum usually starts about 8 years after symptoms begin, with the interval set by extent, activity, PSC and family history (his father's colorectal cancer counts).
points: Chronic bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with weight loss in a young adult is inflammatory bowel disease until proven otherwise; IBS cannot be diagnosed with blood, weight loss, nocturnal stools or a raised calprotectin.

Ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum and limited to the mucosa, with crypt distortion and no granulomas; Crohn's disease has skip lesions, transmural inflammation, granulomas, strictures, fistulae and perianal disease.
Always exclude infection (stool culture or PCR, C. difficile, parasites) before diagnosing or treating a colitis flare.
Grade severity objectively: 6 or more bloody stools a day with fever, HR above 90, Hb below 105 or ESR above 30 is acute severe UC and needs admission.
Mild to moderate distal UC is treated with rectal mesalazine (enema or foam for the sigmoid) combined with oral mesalazine; steroids are added if there is no response.

Complications include toxic megacolon, perforation, haemorrhage and colorectal cancer; extraintestinal manifestations involve joints, eyes, skin (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum) and liver (primary sclerosing cholangitis).
